name: CSEd literature scan
description: >-
  Use when the user wants papers, related work, or a literature scan on computer

---
# CSEd literature scan

## Goal
Produce a usable related-work brief for computer science / programming education research — not a dump of links.

## Steps
1. Clarify the research question in one sentence (topic, population, setting, method if known). If the user already gave it, restate it and proceed without asking.
2. Search the open web for peer-reviewed and high-signal CSEd sources. Prioritize venues and series such as SIGCSE, ICER, ITiCSE, TOCE, Computer Science Education, and well-cited arXiv / conference papers when those are the best available.
3. Prefer primary sources. For each candidate paper note: title, authors, year, venue, one-sentence contribution, method (e.g. classroom study, qualitative, quasi-experiment, tool evaluation), and why it matters to the user's question.
4. Cluster findings into 3–6 themes (e.g. misconceptions, pedagogy, assessment, tools, equity). Under each theme list 2–5 papers with the notes above.
5. Flag gaps: what the literature does not yet answer for this question.
6. End with 3–5 concrete next reads ordered by usefulness, plus one suggested search query the user can reuse.

## Rules
- Never invent citations, DOIs, page numbers, or quotes. If you cannot verify a paper, say so and omit it.
- Distinguish peer-reviewed work from blogs, vendor posts, and opinion pieces.
- Keep the brief skimmable: short paragraphs or tight bullets, no filler.

# Qualitative coding for CSEd

## Goal
Help code qualitative CS education data (student programs, think-alouds, interview transcripts, forum posts, observation notes) into a transparent, reusable codebook.

## Steps
1. Confirm the unit of analysis (line, function, utterance, episode, whole submission) and the research question the codes serve.
2. If no codebook exists, propose an initial codebook: code name, short definition, inclusion/exclusion rules, and 1–2 anonymized example excerpts. Ground codes in the data and in established CSEd constructs when appropriate (e.g. notional machine, tracing vs writing, self-regulation).
3. Apply codes to a first pass of the material the user provided. For each coded unit give: anonymized label, code(s), brief rationale, and a short excerpt.
4. Surface disagreements or ambiguous cases as decision notes the researcher can resolve — do not silently force a code.
5. After a pass, suggest merges, splits, or new codes based on what did not fit. Offer an updated codebook version.
6. Optionally compute simple frequencies or co-occurrence counts from the coded set the user approved.

## Rules
- Never invent student names, IDs, emails, or institutional identifiers. Use labels like S01, Excerpt A.
- Do not claim inter-rater reliability unless the user supplies dual-coded data.
- Treat uploaded student work as confidential research material; do not reuse examples outside this task.

skills.description: Use when designing or reviewing concept inventories, quizzes, or programming assessment items for research or teaching studies.

name: Programming assessment item review
description: >-
  Use when designing or reviewing concept inventories, quizzes, or programming
  assessment items for research or teaching studies.
---
# Programming assessment item review

## Goal
Review or draft programming / CS concept assessment items so they are clearer, fairer, and more useful for research or classroom measurement.

## Steps
1. Identify the construct being measured (e.g. loops, recursion, tracing, debugging, API use) and the intended level (recall, apply, transfer).
2. For each item, check: stem clarity, single correct intent (unless multi-select is deliberate), plausible distractors that map to known misconceptions, language accessibility, and cultural / contextual bias.
3. Map distractors to misconceptions when possible (e.g. off-by-one, reversed condition, confusing = with ==).
4. Suggest revised wording and, when helpful, an alternate isomorphic item for pre/post designs.
5. Note what evidence the item can and cannot support (content validity caveats). Flag items that mainly test reading load or trick phrasing rather than the construct.
6. Deliver a short table or list: item id, construct, issues found, suggested fix, misconception coverage.

## Rules
- Do not claim an item is validated unless the user cites validation evidence.
- Prefer research-aligned language from CSEd assessment literature without fabricating instrument names or statistics.

# CSEd study protocol draft

## Goal
Turn a rough study idea in programming education into a clear protocol outline the researcher can refine for collaborators, advisors, or ethics review.

## Steps
1. Capture: research questions, population, setting (course, lab, online), design (observational, quasi-experiment, RCT, design-based research, qualitative case), and primary measures.
2. Draft sections: background in 1 short paragraph, RQs, participants and recruitment, materials / instruments, procedure, data sources, analysis plan, risks and mitigations, timeline.
3. Call out ethics touchpoints: consent, minors if relevant, deception, data retention, anonymization of student code and grades, instructor dual-role conflicts.
4. List assumptions and open decisions the researcher still needs to make.
5. Offer a one-page plain-language summary suitable for sharing with a teaching team.

## Rules
- This is a drafting aid, not legal or IRB approval. Say that once, plainly.
- Do not invent institutional policy, approval numbers, or effect sizes.
- Prefer concrete, checkable steps over vague methodology slogans.

routines.name: Weekly CSEd lit digest
routines.description: Every Monday morning, deliver a short digest of new programming education research worth reading.
routines.content:
Run a short computer science / programming education literature digest for the user. Search for noteworthy new or newly prominent papers and preprints relevant to programming education research (pedagogy, misconceptions, assessment, tools, equity, LLM-in-CSEd). Prefer SIGCSE, ICER, ITiCSE, TOCE, and similar venues. Send a brief weekday digest: 3–5 items with title, year/venue if known, one-sentence why it matters, and a link when available. Never invent papers. If nothing useful turned up, say so in one line and stay quiet otherwise. Ask once what focus topics to track if none are saved in memory yet; otherwise use the saved focus.
